about.title: Sources & method
about.lead: How the verdict is made, how far to trust it, and where the data comes from.

how.title: How it works
how.body:
Each game lists minimum and, often, recommended requirements on Steam. We recognise the processors and graphics cards named, give each a gaming performance score, then compare them with your PC, component by component. When several models are offered ("GTX 1060 or RX 580"), the weakest sets the bar.
Scores combine published specs (compute power, memory bandwidth, clocks, cores) with per-architecture factors calibrated on well-established gaming equivalences — including those publishers themselves state in their requirements.

levels.title: Verdicts
levels.body:
Meets recommended: your PC meets the recommended requirements.
Meets minimum: the game should run, on modest settings.
Borderline: within 10% of the minimum (15% for laptops), inside the margin of error.
Not enough: below the minimum.
Unknown: a requirement is too vague to compare ("2 GHz processor") or part of your PC isn't filled in. We'd rather say "Unknown" than show a false "Meets recommended".

limits.title: Limits
limits.body:
Scores are estimates (about ±20%): they don't replace a benchmark. Publishers' requirements are themselves approximate, sometimes dated. Frame rates are estimates: we assume a game's minimum requirements aim for ~30 FPS on low settings and the recommended ones for ~60 FPS on high (1080p), then compare your graphics card with the ones asked for. The processor only lowers the estimate when it is below the minimum, as publishers often overstate the recommended one.
Spotted wrong data? The "Report an error" link at the bottom of each game page opens an issue on GitHub.

sources.title: Sources & licences
sources.body: System requirements and images: Steam, loaded from Steam. When Steam doesn't name a processor or graphics card precisely: PCGamingWiki, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. Popular games list: SteamSpy (selection only). Games outside Steam (League of Legends, Valorant, Fortnite…): requirements from PCGamingWiki, images and official site from IGDB. Linux support: Linux versions as listed by Steam or PCGamingWiki, player ratings from ProtonDB (ODbL), anti-cheat status from AreWeAntiCheatYet (MIT). Hardware specs: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0; the derived catalog is published under the same licence. This site is not affiliated with Valve or any publisher. Source code (MIT): github.com/OzawaKyo/can-i-run-it.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.body: Your PC details stay in your browser: nothing is sent to a server. Graphics card detection runs locally, through WebGL. No account, no cookies, no analytics. Only game images are loaded from Steam's servers.

detect.title: Automatic detection
detect.intro: One click fills in your graphics card, then 3 steps detect everything else.
detect.otherOs: Full detection works on Windows and Linux. On another system, fill in the fields below.
detect.step2Windows: Open PowerShell: right-click the Start menu › “Terminal” (or “Windows PowerShell”). Paste with Ctrl+V, then press Enter.
detect.step2HintWindows: It runs in a second and copies the result.
detect.step2Linux: Open a terminal (Ctrl+Alt+T on most distributions). Paste with Ctrl+Shift+V, then press Enter.
detect.step2HintLinux: It runs in a second and prints the result, which it also copies if wl-copy, xclip or xsel is installed. Otherwise, select the line starting with “can-i-run-it:” (or the whole terminal output) and copy it with Ctrl+Shift+C.
detect.step3: Come back here and paste with Ctrl+V (or the button below).
detect.pasteError: That isn't a detection result: run the command again, then paste.
detect.whatItDoesBody: It only reads the processor and graphics card names, installed memory, and the free space and type of the roomiest drive. It installs nothing, changes nothing and sends nothing: the result goes to your clipboard (or is printed in the terminal), and you paste it here yourself.
